newsitem.title: UK: Londoner hot favourite for British literary prize.
newsitem.headline: Londoner hot favourite for British literary prize.

text.p: Londoner Graham Swift is hot favourite to land Britain's top literary prize with "Last Orders", the bizarre tale of a butcher who wants his ashes scattered at sea.
"If the Booker Prize was decided by betting popularity, Swift would be an absolute certainty," said a spokesman for bookmakers Ladbrokes.
They have installed Swift as 4-7 favourite to win the 20,000 pound ($31,930) prize at a glittering dinner on Tuesday night.
The judges read 150 books by writers from 50 Commonwealth countries and Ireland before picking their shortlist of six.
The winner is guaranteed rocketing sales after much pre-ceremony hype and appraisal by literary critics.
"It was a very good year for fiction," said publisher Carmen Callil, who led the panel of judges.

The prize has in the past been dogged by controversy with judges acccused of picking obscure and unreadable books that had no mass appeal. But this year, literary critics have been uncharateristically warm in praise of the choices.
Four of the six authors have been short-listed before.
Beryl Bainbridge, three times a Booker runner-up, hopes to strike it lucky at last with "Every Man for Himself", an evocative recreation of the doomed maiden voyage of The Titanic.

Margaret Atwood, Canada's most acclaimed contemporary novelist, is on the shortlist for the third time. This time she was picked for "Alias Grace", the story of a 19th century servant girl sentenced to hang for a double murder.

Rohinton Mistry, the Bombay-born author who now lives in Canada, is flying over especially for the award, hoping to be crowned for "A Fine Balance", a grim saga of India in the Emergency of the 1970s.
Northern Irish poet Seamus Deane makes it to the list with his first novel -- "Reading in the Dark", a sinister story of a family haunted by a guilty Irish Republican Army secret.
The bookmakers make Shena Mackay the outsider of the party at 9-1 for her Fifties depiction of rural England -- "The Orchard on Fire."

Swift was shortlisted in 1983 for "Waterland". After taking some hefty bets, bookmakers are convinced he will now win with the saga of four feuding friends heading to the seaside with the casket of their late lamented friend.
